items.title: Bounded signed integrals obey the density formula
items.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a positive measure, let $p:X\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued
and measurable, and suppose $P(A)=\int_Ap\,d\mu$ is a probability measure.
If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable and $|f|\le M$ for some finite
$M\ge0$, then $f$ is integrable under $P$, $fp$ is integrable under $\mu$,
and
$$\int_X f\,dP=\int_X fp\,d\mu.$$
items.strategy: Apply the nonnegative density formula to positive and negative parts and subtract their finite integrals.

references.title: Gerald B. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., §§2.2–2.3, PDF pp. 49–54

items.title: A likelihood-ratio threshold with boundary randomization exists
items.statement:
Let $Q$ be a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$, and let
$T:X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function. For every
$\alpha\in(0,1]$, there exist $c\in[0,\infty)$ and
$\gamma\in[0,1]$ such that
$$Q(T>c)+\gamma Q(T=c)=\alpha.$$
items.strategy: Use the upper-tail distribution q(t)=Q(T>t). Continuity from above makes the threshold set nonempty; its infimum gives Q(T>c)≤α≤Q(T≥c). Randomize at the boundary atom, and use γ=0 when the atom is absent.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, §§13.1.1–13.1.2, PDF pp. 76–77
Karl B. Gregory, USC STAT 713 Lecture 11: Neyman–Pearson and Karlin–Rubin, PDF pp. 7–9

items.title: The common-support likelihood ratio is measurable
items.statement:
Let $p_0,p_1:X\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued measurable functions on a
measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. Define
$$R(x)=\begin{cases}p_1(x)/p_0(x),&p_0(x)>0,\\0,&p_0(x)=0.\end{cases}$$
Then $R$ is finite-valued, nonnegative, and measurable.
items.strategy: Define a truncated reciprocal using measurable superlevel sets, then multiply by the alternative density.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, §13.1.2, PDF p. 77
Anna Mikusheva, MIT 14.381 Lecture 9: Uniformly Most Powerful Tests, PDF pp. 2–3

items.title: Valid p-values
items.statement:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

references.title: Karl B. Gregory, USC STAT 713 Lecture 10: Tests of Hypotheses, Size, Power, and p-values, PDF pp. 17–20

items.title: Every measurable rejection function defines a randomized test
items.statement:
Let $\mathsf E=((X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$\varphi:X\to[0,1]$ be measurable, where $[0,1]$ has its Borel sigma-algebra.
On the binary action space $\{0,1\}$ with its full sigma-algebra, define
$$K(x,B)=\varphi(x)\mathbf 1_B(1)+(1-\varphi(x))\mathbf 1_B(0)\qquad (B\subseteq\{0,1\}).$$
Then $K$ is a probability kernel and hence a randomized procedure; its
randomized-test function under the convention $1=\mathrm{reject}$ is
$\varphi$.
items.strategy: Assign the action probabilities φ(x) and 1−φ(x) to the two singleton actions. Check that each section is a probability measure on the finite action space and that its four evaluations are measurable.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §5.1, PDF pp. 100–102
Peter Hoff, Statistical Decision Problems, §§2–4.2, PDF pp. 2–8

items.title: Binary zero-one loss risks are the testing error probabilities
items.statement:
Let $\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be disjoint subsets of a parameter set $\Theta$ in
a statistical experiment. Let $K$ be a randomized test on the binary action
space $\{0,1\}$, with $1$ meaning reject, and write
$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\})$. Define the zero-one error loss by
$$L(\theta,a)=\mathbf 1_{\Theta_0}(\theta)a+\mathbf 1_{\Theta_1}(\theta)(1-a),$$
so $L$ is zero when $\theta\notin\Theta_0\cup\Theta_1$. For
$\beta_\varphi(\theta)=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]$ and the risk
$R(\theta,K)$ of [[def-loss-function-and-risk]],
$$R(\theta,K)=\beta_\varphi(\theta)\quad(\theta\in\Theta_0),\qquad R(\theta,K)=1-\beta_\varphi(\theta)\quad(\theta\in\Theta_1).$$
items.strategy: Evaluate the finite action integral at each data point, then integrate it under the parameter law.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §5.1, PDF pp. 100–102
Peter Hoff, Statistical Decision Problems, §§4.1–4.2, PDF pp. 7–8

items.title: Test size and power
items.statement:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, §§13.1.1–13.1.2, PDF pp. 76–77
Karl B. Gregory, USC STAT 713 Lecture 10: Tests of Hypotheses, Size, Power, and p-values, PDF pp. 2–7

items.title: Likelihood-ratio tests with boundary randomization
items.statement:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\{0,1\},(P_0,P_1))$ be the
two-law statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Assume
$P_0,P_1$ are both absolutely continuous with respect to a supplied
sigma-finite measure $\mu$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$
([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]) and specify finite-valued,
nonnegative measurable RN density representatives $p_0=dP_0/d\mu$ and
$p_1=dP_1/d\mu$ ([[def-likelihood-density]]). Under the Axiom of Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]),
[[def-likelihood-density]] supplies such representatives for arbitrary
dominated laws. If the representatives are given as part of the setup, the
construction below requires no choice.

Define the common-support likelihood ratio
$$R(x)=\begin{cases}p_1(x)/p_0(x),&p_0(x)>0,\\0,&p_0(x)=0.\end{cases}$$
The result [[lem-common-support-likelihood-ratio-is-measurable]] shows that
$R$ is finite-valued, nonnegative, and measurable. The set
$\{p_0=0<p_1\}$ is kept separate from the ratio region.

For $\alpha=0$, define the rejection function
$$\varphi^*_0(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p_0=0<p_1\}}(x).$$
For $0<\alpha\le1$, choose $c\ge0$ and $\gamma\in[0,1]$ satisfying
$$P_0(R>c)+\gamma P_0(R=c)=\alpha,$$
whose existence follows from
[[lem-likelihood-ratio-threshold-exists]] applied to $Q=P_0$ and $T=R$.
Define
$$
\varphi^*_\alpha(x)=\begin{cases}1,&p_0(x)=0<p_1(x),\\1,&p_0(x)>0\text{ and }R(x)>c,\\\gamma,&p_0(x)>0\text{ and }R(x)=c,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
$$
This specifies the candidate likelihood-ratio rejection function.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, §13.1.2, PDF p. 77
Anna Mikusheva, MIT 14.381 Lecture 9: Uniformly Most Powerful Tests, PDF pp. 2–3
Karl B. Gregory, USC STAT 713 Lecture 11: Neyman–Pearson and Karlin–Rubin, PDF pp. 7–9

items.title: Valid p-values yield level tests for nonempty disjoint alternatives
items.statement:
Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
has size at most $\alpha$, and therefore has level $\alpha$.
items.strategy: Use measurability of the sublevel set and identify the rejection probability under each null parameter with the p-value tail probability.

references.title: Karl B. Gregory, USC STAT 713 Lecture 10: Tests of Hypotheses, Size, Power, and p-values, PDF pp. 17–20

items.title: The likelihood-ratio rule is a measurable test of exact size
items.statement:
In the setup of [[def-likelihood-ratio-test-with-boundary-randomization]],
for every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ the candidate rejection function
$\varphi^*_\alpha$ is measurable into $[0,1]$, defines a randomized test,
and has size exactly $\alpha$ for the simple null $P_0$.
items.strategy: Show the candidate is a finite sum of measurable indicators and compute its null expectation from the threshold equation.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, §13.1.2, PDF p. 77
Anna Mikusheva, MIT 14.381 Lecture 9: Uniformly Most Powerful Tests, PDF pp. 2–3

items.title: Neyman–Pearson lemma with singular alternative mass
items.statement:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\{0,1\},(P_0,P_1))$ be the
two-law experiment with simple null $P_0$ and simple alternative $P_1$.
Assume both laws are dominated by a common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ and
assume the Axiom of Choice, so finite nonnegative density representatives
$p_0,p_1$ are supplied by [[def-likelihood-density]]. For every
$\alpha\in[0,1]$, let $\varphi_\alpha^*$ be the likelihood-ratio test with
boundary randomization from
[[def-likelihood-ratio-test-with-boundary-randomization]]. Then every
randomized test $\varphi$ satisfying
$E_{P_0}[\varphi(X)]\le\alpha$ also satisfies
$$E_{P_1}[\varphi(X)]\le E_{P_1}[\varphi_\alpha^*(X)].$$
No absolute-continuity assumption $P_1\ll P_0$ is imposed; the test rejects
on $\{p_0=0<p_1\}$.
items.strategy: On the common-density support, the sign of (φ*−φ)(p1−cp0) is nonnegative. The P0-null set {p0=0<p1} contributes nonnegative power separately. Integrate and use exact size α; handle α=0 by showing a level-zero competitor vanishes P1-a.e. on {p0>0}.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 13, §13.1.2, PDF p. 77
Anna Mikusheva, MIT 14.381 Lecture 9: Uniformly Most Powerful Tests, PDF pp. 2–3
Karl B. Gregory, USC STAT 713 Lecture 11: Neyman–Pearson and Karlin–Rubin, PDF pp. 7–9

title: Tests, Neyman–Pearson and Valid P-values — Examples

items.title: A measurable [0,1]-valued statistic need not be a valid p-value
items.statement:
Every measurable statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ is a valid p-value for a
given null hypothesis.
items.strategy: Use a two-point null law and a statistic that is zero on an event of probability one half. Its rejection probability at α=1/4 is one half.

items.title: Randomize at a discrete likelihood-ratio boundary
items.statement:
On $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with its full sigma-algebra and counting measure
$\mu$, let the simple null and alternative laws be
$P_0(\{0\})=P_0(\{1\})=1/2$ and
$P_1(\{0\})=1/4$, $P_1(\{1\})=3/4$. At level $\alpha=1/4$, the
Neyman–Pearson test randomizes with probability $1/2$ at $x=1$ and rejects
with probability $0$ at $x=0$. Its size is $1/4$ and its power is $3/8$.
items.strategy: Compute the two likelihood ratios, solve the boundary equation, and integrate the rejection function under P0 and P1.

items.title: A continuous likelihood-ratio test
items.statement:
On $[0,1]$ with restricted Lebesgue measure, let $P_0$ have density
$p_0(x)=1$ and let $P_1$ have density $p_1(x)=2x$. At level
$\alpha=1/4$, the likelihood-ratio test rejects for $x>3/4$, has size
$1/4$, and has power $7/16$.
items.strategy: Verify both densities, calculate p1/p0=2x, and integrate over the upper-tail rejection region.
